slides.slide_purpose: Introduce the novel task of automated To-Do generation from emails
content_points: Novel application: Generating actionable To-Do items from email commitments
Key challenges: Email thread diversity, structural heterogeneity, and metadata complexity
Differentiation: Action-focused generation vs. traditional text summarization
Core objective: Identify task sentences, contextual information, and associated entities

images.caption: Figure 1: An illustration showing the email and a commitment sentence (in yellow) and the target To-Do item, along with other email meta-data.
images.analysis_text: Figure 1 illustrates the core components involved in generating a To-Do item from an email, highlighting a commitment sentence (marked in yellow) that indicates a promised action by the sender. The figure shows how this sentence, along with surrounding email content and metadata such as sender and recipient information, is used to derive a concise and actionable To-Do item. This visual representation underscores the system's goal of extracting task-relevant information from natural language email text to support user productivity through automated task creation.

slides.slide_purpose: Present the end-to-end framework for To-Do item generation
content_points: Two-stage process: Commitment detection followed by neural generation
Component 1: Commitment classifier identifies action-intent sentences
Component 2: Unsupervised extraction of contextual sentences
Component 3: Sequence-to-sequence architecture for final output generation

images.caption: Figure 2: Smart To-Do flowchart: The email content is first scanned to detect any possible commitment sentence. If present, a To-Do item is generated using a two-stage Smart To-Do framework.
images.analysis_text: Figure 2 illustrates the Smart-To-Do framework, which automates the generation of To-Do items from emails containing commitments. The process begins with scanning email content to detect commitment sentences—indications that the sender has promised to perform an action. Once a commitment is identified, the system proceeds to generate a concise To-Do item using a two-stage approach: first extracting relevant contextual information and key entities, then applying a sequence-to-sequence neural model to produce the final task description. This flowchart highlights the integration of commitment detection, context extraction, and neural text generation to support intelligent task management in email environments.

slides.section_name: 4.1 Identifying Helpful Sentences for Commitment Task
slides.slide_purpose: Introduce the unsupervised matching-based method for identifying helpful sentences in emails.
content_points: Leverage unsupervised matching to score sentences for relevance to commitment.
Define commitment sentence as query and other sentences as candidates.
Compute relevance score Ω(s_i) for each sentence based on semantic similarity.
Select top K sentences as extractive summary for commitment context.

slides.section_name: 4.1 Identifying Helpful Sentences for Commitment Task
slides.slide_purpose: Detail the process of creating an enriched context for relevance scoring.
content_points: Extract top τ (τ=10) most frequent tokens from email, commitment, and subject.
Lemmatize tokens and remove stop-words for cleaner context.
Form enriched context E by concatenating commitment, subject, and top tokens.
Use enriched context to compute semantic similarity with candidate sentences.

slides.section_name: 4.1 Identifying Helpful Sentences for Commitment Task
slides.slide_purpose: Explain the mathematical foundation of the relevance scoring mechanism.
content_points: Compute Ω(s_i) as inner product in embedding space: h(s_i)^T h(E).
Evaluate three embedding functions: Term-frequency, FastText, and BERT.
Semantic similarity ensures alignment between enriched context and target sentence.
Subject and email topic compensate for short or less informative queries.

slides.section_name: 4.1 Identifying Helpful Sentences for Commitment Task
slides.slide_purpose: Present empirical results comparing different embedding methods.
content_points: Measure proportion of emails with at least one helpful sentence in top K.
FastText (Max) outperforms others: 0.85 (K=2) and 0.92 (K=3).
Simple embedding methods surpass BERT without labeled supervision.
70.4% of replied-to emails contain helpful sentences in previous email body.

tables.caption: Table 2: Performance of unsupervised approaches in identifying helpful sentences for a given query.
tables.analysis_text: Table 2 evaluates the performance of various unsupervised approaches in identifying at least one helpful sentence from an email thread, which is crucial for enriching the context of a To-Do item generated from a commitment sentence. The metrics report the proportion of emails where at least one helpful sentence appears among the top K retrieved sentences (K=2 and K=3). Among the methods tested—Term Frequency (Tf), FastText with mean and max pooling, and pre-trained and fine-tuned BERT—the FastText (Max) approach achieves the highest scores: 0.85 at K=2 and 0.92 at K=3. This indicates that max-pooling over FastText embeddings effectively captures relevant contextual information. The results highlight that even simple embedding-based methods outperform more complex models like BERT when no labeled data is used for supervision, underscoring the effectiveness of the proposed unsupervised relevance scoring strategy.

slides.section_name: 4.1 Identifying Helpful Sentences for Commitment Task
slides.slide_purpose: Describe the generation stage leveraging the identified helpful sentences.
content_points: Sequence-to-sequence model with copy mechanism for To-Do generation.
Directly copies named entities and task-specific keywords from input.
Ensures fidelity between email content and generated task.
Supports reliable task management by preserving critical information.

images.caption: Figure 3: Seq2Seq with copy mechanism. Tokens involving named entities and task-specific keywords from the email are learned to copy in the To-Do item.
images.analysis_text: Figure 3 illustrates a sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) model with a copy mechanism designed to generate To-Do items from emails. This architecture enables the model to directly copy important tokens—such as named entities and task-specific keywords—from the input email into the generated To-Do item, preserving critical information that may be otherwise lost during generation. The copy mechanism enhances the model's ability to accurately reflect commitments made in the email, especially when dealing with proper nouns or specific actions mentioned in the source text. This approach is particularly useful for ensuring fidelity between the original email content and the generated task, supporting more reliable task management.

slides.slide_purpose: Introduce the core architecture of the To-Do item generation system
content_points: Problem framed as Seq2Seq learning with attention mechanisms
Encoder processes concatenated email metadata: recipient, subject, commitment sentences
Decoder generates To-Do items using attention over encoder states
Special markers distinguish different input components

equations.analysis_text: This equation represents the input format used in the encoder of the sequence-to-sequence model for generating To-Do items from emails. It shows a structured concatenation of email metadata fields—such as 'to', 'subject', 'query', and 'sent'—separated by special tokens (e.g., <to>, <sub>, <query>, <sent>) to distinguish different components. The example illustrates how the system processes an email where the sender promises to send a document, with the query asking for it and the commitment sentence indicating intent. This structured input allows the model to capture relevant contextual information across different parts of the email, enabling effective task extraction and To-Do item generation.

slides.slide_title: Model Variants: From Vanilla to Advanced Architectures
slides.slide_purpose: Compare different model configurations for task generation
content_points: Baseline: Vanilla Seq2Seq with single LSTM encoder-decoder
Enhanced version with attention mechanism for focused context
Copy mechanism variant for preserving key entities (names, dates)
BiFocal architecture with dual encoders for query/context separation

equations.analysis_text: This equation defines the attention mechanism used in the sequence-to-sequence model for generating To-Do items from emails. The first line computes an alignment score $ e_{t,t'} $ between the decoder state at timestep $ t $ and the encoder hidden state at timestep $ t' $, using a feed-forward network with learned parameters $ W_h $, $ W_s $, and bias $ b $. The second line applies softmax to obtain the attention weights $ a_{t,t'} $, which represent how much the decoder should focus on each encoder state when generating the next word. The third line computes the context vector $ h_t $ as a weighted sum of the encoder hidden states, where the weights are given by the attention distribution. This allows the decoder to dynamically focus on relevant parts of the email input—such as key entities or commitments—when generating meaningful To-Do items.

slides.slide_purpose: Present empirical evaluation of model effectiveness
content_points: Copy mechanism achieves highest scores (BLEU-4: 0.23, ROUGE-L: 0.63)
Significant improvement over vanilla Seq2Seq baseline
Human judgment baseline provides competitive upper bound
Concatenation approach performs worst, validating neural design

tables.caption: Table 4: Comparison of various models for To-Do generation with BLEU and ROUGE (higher is better).
tables.analysis_text: Table 4 compares the performance of several sequence-to-sequence models for generating To-Do items from emails, using BLEU-4 and ROUGE metrics (higher values indicate better performance). The results show that the Seq2Seq model with copy mechanism achieves the highest scores across all metrics—BLEU-4 of 0.23, ROUGE-1 of 0.60, ROUGE-2 of 0.41, and ROUGE-L of 0.63—outperforming both the vanilla Seq2Seq and BiFocal variants. This highlights the importance of the copy mechanism in preserving key entities such as names, dates, and tasks directly from the email context. Notably, the human judgment baseline achieves competitive scores, suggesting that automated generation can approach human-level performance. The Concatenate baseline, which simply concatenates relevant email parts without modeling, performs the worst, underscoring the need for structured neural approaches in this task.

tables.caption: Table 5: Seq2Seq with copy mechanism : Hyperparameters for the best model.
tables.analysis_text: Table 5 presents the hyperparameters of the best-performing sequence-to-sequence model with a copy mechanism used for generating To-Do items from emails. Key architectural choices include an LSTM-based encoder-decoder with a single layer and 256 hidden units, word embeddings initialized using Glove vectors (100-dimensional), and a separate vocabulary for source and target sequences to improve performance and avoid overfitting. Training was conducted with a batch size of 64, Adagrad optimizer at a learning rate of 0.15, and gradient clipping set to a maximum norm of 2.0. Dropout and attention dropout were both set to 0.5 to regularize the model. The tokenizer used was spaCy, and early stopping was applied with a patience of 5 epochs based on validation token accuracy or perplexity. Beam search with width 5 was used during inference. These settings reflect a carefully tuned configuration that balances model capacity, training stability, and generalization for the task of email-based To-Do generation.

tables.analysis_text: Table 6 presents an illustrative example of an email thread where a sender (Beverly Evans) requests action from the recipient (Carlos Simmons), followed by Carlos's response. The goal is to automatically generate a To-Do item based on the commitments made in the conversation. The 'GOLD' entry shows the human-annotated correct To-Do item: 'Forward PHP example to Beverly and Renata,' which captures the explicit action requested in Carlos's email. In contrast, the model's prediction ('PRED') is 'Forward eCommerce PHP to Beverly,' which is partially accurate but misses the mention of Renata and incorrectly specifies 'eCommerce PHP' instead of the 'relevant PHP example' referenced in the message. This highlights the challenge of accurately extracting and summarizing actionable tasks from nuanced email content, especially when dealing with ambiguous or indirect references.

How can I do this? What is the way to perform this operation? Also, in the bash script, is there a way to sort the dates so that we can identify older activities? Thanks, Rebecca.
From: Julia Roberts To: Rebecca Anderson Subject: Run a bash script while synchronize Rebecca, We had exactly the same feature to delete activities which you mentioned in our previous release. But we no longer have that in the new version due to resource constraints. I will take to John to review this again. Thanks, Julia.
GOLD: Talk to John to review bash script again.
PRED: Talk to John to review the activities.
tables.analysis_text: Table 10 presents an illustrative example of an email thread where the sender, Rebecca Anderson, requests guidance on running a bash script during synchronization, and the recipient, Julia Roberts, responds by mentioning that a similar feature was removed due to resource constraints and commits to discussing it with John. The gold-standard To-Do item, created by a human judge, is 'Talk to John to review bash script again,' capturing the key action committed to by Julia. The model's prediction, 'Talk to John to review the activities,' reflects a reasonable but slightly less precise interpretation, as it generalizes 'bash script' to 'activities.' This example highlights the challenge of accurately extracting actionable commitments from natural language emails, especially when contextual details are implicit or paraphrased.

slides.slide_title: Example 6: Salient but Incorrect Information Focus
slides.slide_purpose: Demonstrate the model's tendency to focus on incorrect salient information.
content_points: Sender: Ramesh Paul commits to sending details.
GOLD: 'Send Gopal more details about tests in the desktop for v5'.
PRED: 'Send Gopal more details on presentation for the knowledge transfer'.
Model captures related but incorrect action.

tables.caption: Table 11: Illustrative Example 6
tables.body:
From: Ramesh Paul To: Gopal Majumdar Subject: Updates List for 3/11 Here's the update for this week. 1. The R&D team is working on a presentation for the knowledge tranfer for v5. It should be ready within next two weeks. 2. I have received their email, but need to review the ppt. 3. Did you want to know more about the new cloud feature for automatic version management ? Or was it a different feature ? 4. I am constantly working on this. 5. Didn't we discuss this point in our last email ? 6. We are making similar tests in the desktop for v5 before migrating to the cloud. We first have to make sure things work well for the desktop. I will send you more details soon. Did you get a chance to update your blog with information about these new features ? Thanks, Ramesh.
GOLD: Send Gopal more details about tests in the desktop for v5.
PRED: Send Gopal more details on presentation for the knowledge transfer.
tables.analysis_text: This table presents an illustrative example of an email from Ramesh Paul to Gopal Majumdar, containing multiple sentences that discuss ongoing work and commitments. The key commitment is in the sentence 'I will send you more details soon,' which leads to a To-Do item. The GOLD label represents the human-generated To-Do item: 'Send Gopal more details about tests in the desktop for v5,' reflecting the actual action promised. In contrast, the PRED (predicted) To-Do item generated by the model is 'Send Gopal more details on presentation for the knowledge transfer,' which captures a related but incorrect action based on a different part of the email. This highlights a challenge in accurately identifying the correct commitment sentence and generating precise task items, demonstrating the model's tendency to focus on salient but not necessarily relevant information.

slides.slide_purpose: Highlight the challenge of capturing contextual nuances.
content_points: Sender: Lori Howard mentions pending action on training.
GOLD: 'Let Karen know about the training provide for room reservations'.
PRED: 'Let Karen know about room reservations'.
Model omits mention of training.

tables.caption: Table 12: Illustrative Example 7
tables.body:
From: Lori Howard To: Karen James; Bruce Thomas; Steve Perry Subject: Room reservations Team, This needs to be done through a formal training session, but as of now let me point out some crucial points about room reservations. 1. In case you allocate a room for general meetings and administrative work, then make sure you book it for that month, but not for long periods of time. (Karen, can you check with Renata whether this is fulfilled for our meetings next week?) 2. In case of clients who do not need the entire month, make sure to reserve only for the particular month. If it exceeds that time, the system will automatically resolve it and reserve it for next month. 3. For room reservation, either enter the number of hours required or the % of month, but not both. I would prefer precise hours. I will inform you when we can provide training, perhaps we can next week. Thanks, Lori.
GOLD: Let Karen know about the training provide for room reservations.
PRED: Let Karen know about room reservations.
tables.analysis_text: Table 12 presents an illustrative example of an email where the sender, Lori Howard, mentions a pending action related to training for room reservations and specifically asks Karen to check with Renata about meeting arrangements. The 'GOLD' entry shows the human-generated To-Do item: 'Let Karen know about the training provide for room reservations,' which captures the intended task accurately. The model's prediction ('PRED') is slightly less complete, stating 'Let Karen know about room reservations,' omitting the mention of training. This comparison highlights the challenge in fully capturing contextual nuances in commitments from emails, even when the core action is identified correctly.

slides.slide_purpose: Showcase a case where the model partially captures the task scope.
content_points: Sender: Matthew White commits to preparing a training plan.
GOLD: 'Put together the training plan and the overall day agenda of software training'.
PRED: 'Put together the draft agenda for software training'.
Model misses broader scope of the task.

tables.caption: Table 13: Illustrative Example 8
tables.body:
From: Matthew White To: Frank; Paul; Dennis Subject: Draft Agenda for Software Training Dear All, As discussed before, we have finally come to a concrete plan. I have attached the draft for your review. Please go over it and let me know asap your suggestions so that I can send them to the organizers. Please check the agenda and the names of trainees. I'll put together the Training plan and the overall 5-day agenda as soon as I can. Matthew.
GOLD: Put together the training plan and the overall day agenda of software training.
PRED: Put together the draft agenda for software training.
tables.analysis_text: This table presents an illustrative example of an email where the sender, Matthew White, commits to preparing a training plan and agenda. The 'GOLD' entry shows the human-annotated To-Do item that accurately captures the action promised in the email: 'Put together the training plan and the overall day agenda of software training.' In contrast, the model's prediction ('PRED') is less precise, stating 'Put together the draft agenda for software training,' which misses the broader scope of the task including the full 5-day plan. This comparison highlights the challenge of generating comprehensive and accurate To-Do items from emails, demonstrating that while the model captures part of the commitment, it falls short in fully understanding and paraphrasing the complete intent.

slides.slide_purpose: Demonstrate the model's ability to identify implicit action items.
content_points: Sender: Diana Wilson tracks a DHL package.
GOLD and PRED: 'Let Diana know about DHL package from IBM'.
Model successfully extracts implicit task commitment.

tables.caption: Table 14: Illustrative Example 9
tables.body:
From: Diana Wilson To: Alba Deacon Subject: DHL package from IBM Alba, I was able to track the package and as per the website it was in Sao Luis, Brazil at noon. I am not sure where it is, but it is Brazil so ... Send me an update if you receive it from them. I just tracked the package and as of 10:00am today it was in Toluca, Mexico. Where that is I have no idea but it is in Mexico so ... Let me know if you hear from them when they receive it. Thanks. Diana Wilson.
From: Alba Deacon To: Diana Wilson Subject: DHL package from IBM Thanks Diana. If I hear anything I'll let you know. Alba.
GOLD: Let Diana know about DHL package from IBM.
PRED: Let Diana know about DHL package from IBM.
tables.analysis_text: Table 14 presents an illustrative example of an email thread where a sender, Diana Wilson, tracks a DHL package and requests updates from Alba Deacon. The exchange includes multiple messages indicating ongoing communication about the package's status. The gold-standard To-Do item, generated by a human judge, is 'Let Diana know about DHL package from IBM,' which captures the recipient’s obligation to inform Diana upon receiving updates. The model’s prediction matches exactly, demonstrating successful extraction of the task commitment from the email content. This example highlights the system's ability to identify implicit action items in natural email conversations, even when the language is informal or contains uncertainty.

slides.slide_purpose: Summarize the insights gained from the examples.
content_points: Model captures core actions but varies in detail preservation.
Challenges include contextual specificity and intent fidelity.
Successful in implicit task extraction but prone to generalization.
Room for improvement in comprehensive task understanding.
